hints: Think about what must happen for a cancer cell to divide uncontrollably, and which large molecule must be copied exactly.
Consider how a small platinum complex that can form coordinate bonds to nitrogen atoms in bases could interfere with that copying process.
walkthrough:
Picture the target in a cancer cell**
Cancer is uncontrolled cell division. To divide, a cell must first make an exact copy of its DNA by replication, and also use DNA to make mRNA by transcription. Anything that locks up the DNA stops both processes.

See how cisplatin locks the DNA**
Inside the cell cisplatin loses its chloride ligands and the platinum centre forms strong coordinate bonds to nitrogen atoms on the DNA bases. The complex bridges across the strands and distorts the double helix. With the DNA chemically blocked and bent out of shape, the enzymes for replication and transcription cannot work, so the cell cannot divide and dies.

Final answer: Cisplatin binds / bonds to DNA / to nitrogenous bases (A, T, C, G).
This prevents replication of DNA / prevents transcription to mRNA / prevents cell division by mitosis.

hints: Count the donor atoms bonded to Pt in carboplatin and recall the characteristic shape for 4 coordinate Pt(II) complexes.
walkthrough:
Count donors and recall Pt(II)**
Look at carboplatin: Pt is bonded to two $\text{NH}_3$ nitrogens and two carboxylate oxygens, so coordination number is 4. Platinum(II) with coordination number 4 is almost always square planar, with all four donor atoms and Pt in one plane at $90^{\circ}$ to each other.

hints: Look at the dicarboxylate ligand in carboplatin and notice that its two O donor atoms are joined together in one chelate ring.
walkthrough:
Why a chelate cannot stretch across**
Cis-trans isomerism needs two separate identical ligands that can swap between $90^{\circ}$ apart and $180^{\circ}$ apart. Here the two O donors belong to one bidentate dicarboxylate that forms a 6 membered chelate ring with Pt. The carbon backbone holds the two O atoms close together, so they can only bite at $90^{\circ}$ in cis positions and can never reach opposite sides of the square.

Final answer: The two coordinating O atoms are part of the same bidentate ligand and can only occupy adjacent (cis, $90^{\circ}$) positions, they are too close together to span trans ($180^{\circ}$) positions.

hints: Add up the total negative charge from the anionic ligands ($\text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2^-$ and $\text{Cl}^-$) and remember the amine ligands are neutral and the overall complex is neutral.
walkthrough:
Balance charges to find Pt**
Let the oxidation state of Pt be $x$. Ligands: $2 \times \text{CH}_3\text{CO}_2^-$ gives $2 \times (-1) = -2$, $2 \times \text{Cl}^-$ gives $2 \times (-1) = -2$, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{11}\text{NH}_2$ and $\text{NH}_3$ are neutral ($0$). For a neutral complex: $$x + (-2) + (-2) + 0 + 0 = 0$$ so $$x = +4$$

hints: Compare the starting material and product M, both have 1,3 substitution, and use the formula $\text{C}_8\text{H}_6\text{O}_4$ to work out what functional group L must contain.
walkthrough:
Read the carbon skeleton**
1,3-dimethylbenzene has two $\text{-CH}_3$ groups meta to each other. M has two $\text{-COCl}$ groups meta to each other. So step 1 must convert $\text{-CH}_3$ to a group that step 2 can convert to $\text{-COCl}$. The formula $\text{C}_8\text{H}_6\text{O}_4$ fits a benzene ring ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_4$) plus two $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ groups ($\text{C}_2\text{H}_2\text{O}_4$). That is exactly benzene-1,3-dicarboxylic acid, keeping the same 1,3 pattern.
Final answer: L is benzene-1,3-dicarboxylic acid, $1,3\text{-HO}_2\text{C-C}_6\text{H}_4\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ with two $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ groups in meta positions.

hints: Recall the strong oxidising agent that converts alkyl side chains on a benzene ring completely to $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ with heating.
Recall the chlorinating reagents that replace the $\text{-OH}$ of a carboxylic acid by $\text{-Cl}$ to give an acyl chloride.
walkthrough:
Oxidise methyl to carboxylic acid**
Alkylbenzenes resist mild oxidation, but hot concentrated $\text{KMnO}_4$ cleaves the whole side chain to $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$. Heating 1,3-dimethylbenzene under reflux with acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$, or with alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$ followed by dilute acid to protonate the carboxylate salt, gives L.

Convert acid to acyl chloride**
The $\text{-OH}$ in $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ is replaced by $\text{-Cl}$ using a chlorinating agent. $\text{PCl}_5$ at room temperature, or $\text{SOCl}_2$, or heating with $\text{PCl}_3$, converts each $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ to $\text{-COCl}$ to give the diacyl chloride M.

Final answer: step 1: heat / reflux with acidified or alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$, then acidify if alkaline
step 2: $\text{PCl}_5$ or $\text{SOCl}_2$ or $\text{PCl}_3$ with heat

hints: Write L as $\text{C}_8\text{H}_6\text{O}_4$ and M as $\text{C}_8\text{H}_4\text{O}_2\text{Cl}_2$, then balance the chosen chlorinating agent and its characteristic inorganic products.
walkthrough:
Balance two acid groups**
Each $\text{-CO}_2\text{H}$ needs one $\text{PCl}_5$ to become $\text{-COCl}$. So one mole of diacid L needs two moles of $\text{PCl}_5$: $$\text{C}_8\text{H}_6\text{O}_4 + 2\text{PCl}_5 \rightarrow \text{C}_8\text{H}_4\text{O}_2\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{POCl}_3 + 2\text{HCl}$$ The same logic with $\text{SOCl}_2$ gives $2\text{SO}_2 + 2\text{HCl}$ as byproducts. Check atoms: $\text{C}_8$, $\text{H}_6$, $\text{O}_4$, $\text{P}_2$, $\text{Cl}_{10}$ balance on both sides.

hints: Start the mechanism by identifying the electrophile $\text{Cl-C}^+\text{=O}$ and the nucleophile, which is the pi electron cloud of the benzene ring.
Recall that the first step of electrophilic substitution breaks aromaticity to give a positively charged arenium (Wheland) intermediate with the new C-C bond.
Think about how aromaticity is restored in the final step by removing a proton from the same carbon that was attacked.
walkthrough:
Attack of the ring on the acylium ion**
Treat $\text{Cl-}\overset{+}{\text{C}}\text{=O}$ as the electrophile, with a strongly $\delta+$ carbon. Draw a curly arrow starting from the pi electrons inside the benzene hexagon and pointing to that electrophilic carbon. This forms a new $\text{C-C}$ bond between the ring and the $\text{C=O}$ carbon.

Draw the Wheland intermediate correctly**
Attack breaks the aromatic sextet. The ring becomes a cyclohexadienyl cation with the positive charge delocalised over the remaining five carbons, often drawn with a horseshoe and + sign, plus the $\text{-C(=O)Cl}$ group and the original H both attached to the $sp^3$ carbon. Do not lose $\text{H}^+$ yet.

Restore aromaticity by deprotonation**
Now draw a curly arrow from the $\text{C-H}$ bond at the attacked carbon back into the ring to reform the pi system. The H leaves as $\text{H}^+$. This restores the stable aromatic benzene ring, giving $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl}$. This two step addition then elimination pattern is the hallmark of electrophilic aromatic substitution.

Final answer: Curly arrow from benzene pi system (inside hexagon) to C of $\text{Cl-C}^+\text{=O}$ electrophile to form arenium intermediate with new C-C bond and positive charge delocalised in ring.
Intermediate shows $\text{-C(=O)Cl}$ bonded to a cyclohexadienyl cation with H still attached to that carbon.
Curly arrow from $\text{C-H}$ bond back into ring to reform aromatic pi system, loss of $\text{H}^+$ to give $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCl}$.
